GenerativeMPC: VLM-RAG-guided Whole-Body MPC with Virtual Impedance for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation Thanks: The authors are with the Intelligent Space Robotics Laboratory,
Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology, Moscow, Russia.
{Marcelino.Fernando,M.Altamirano,
Jeffrin.Sam,Yara.Mahmoud,
Konstantin.Gubernatorov,D.Tsetserukou}
@skoltech.ru

Marcelino Julio Fernando    Miguel Altamirano Cabrera    Jeffrin Sam Affiliation: Yara Mahmoud, Konstantin Gubernatorov, and Dzmitry Tsetserukou
Abstract

Bimanual mobile manipulation requires a seamless integration between high-level semantic reasoning and safe, compliant physical interaction—a challenge that end-to-end models approach opaquely and classical controllers lack the context to address. This paper presents GenerativeMPC, a hierarchical cyber-physical framework that explicitly bridges semantic scene understanding with physical control parameters for bimanual mobile manipulators. The system utilizes a Vision-Language Model with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (VLM-RAG) to translate visual and linguistic context into grounded control constraints, specifically outputting dynamic velocity limits and safety margins for a Whole-Body Model Predictive Controller (MPC). Simultaneously, the VLM-RAG module modulates virtual stiffness and damping gains for a unified impedance-admittance controller, enabling context-aware compliance during human-robot interaction. Our framework leverages an experience-driven vector database to ensure consistent parameter grounding without retraining. Experimental results in MuJoCo, IsaacSim, and on a physical bimanual platform confirm a 60% speed reduction near humans and safe, socially-aware navigation and manipulation through semantic-to-physical parameter grounding. This work advances the field of human-centric cybernetics by grounding large-scale cognitive models into predictable, high-frequency physical control loops.

I Introduction

Autonomous robots operating in human-centered environments must navigate unstructured spaces, manipulate objects with varying compliance requirements, and interpret instructions from non-expert users. Bimanual mobile manipulators, platforms combining a mobile base with two articulated arms, are uniquely positioned to address these demands. However, their complexity exposes a fundamental tension: the semantic richness required for task understanding and the physical precision required for safe interaction have been handled by separate, incompatible systems. This fragmentation prevents the realization of a unified cybernetic loop where high-level cognitive reasoning directly modulates the robot’s physical reflexes.

Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot reasoning over visual scenes  [1, 2]. However, existing VLM-based planners typically output discrete subgoals, leaving physical compliance behavior, how stiff or yielding the robot should be during contact, entirely undefined at the semantic level  [3, 4]. While recent state-of-the-art models like MoManipVLA  [5] and FALCON  [6] have pushed the boundaries of end-to-end mobile manipulation, they primarily focus on kinematic success rather than the modulation of the robot’s physical ’feel’ (stiffness and damping) based on context. Separately, whole-body Model Predictive Control (MPC) frameworks enable real-time trajectory optimization for high degree-of-freedom platforms  [7, 8]. While these methods have achieved impressive results in collision-free locomotion and manipulation  [9], or combined RL-based planning with low-level MPC  [10], the velocity constraints and safety margins that shape their behavior are typically fixed at design time.

The present work addresses the open problem of grounding semantic scene understanding into predictable physical control for bimanual mobile manipulation. Building upon the semantic-to-compliance paradigm established in SafeHumanoid  [11], we extend this logic to a unified cyber-physical framework where whole-body coordination, non-holonomic navigation, and dual-arm compliance are handled jointly.

Furthermore, we address the ”memory gap” in robotics; while Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has transformed natural language processing by grounding outputs in factual context [12], its application to experience-driven control loops remains largely unexplored.

This paper presents GenerativeMPC, a three-layer framework in which a VLM-RAG module (InternVL3-1B [12], ChromaDB [13]) produces two distinct outputs from the camera image and task instruction: (1) velocity limits vmaxv_{\max}, ωmax\omega_{\max} and safety margin dsafed_{\text{safe}} that constrain the Whole-Body MPC, and (2) stiffness KiK_{i} and damping DiD_{i} gains that govern a unified impedance-admittance controller. The MPC plans coordinated trajectories for the base and both arms at 10 Hz over N=7N=7 steps, with obstacle avoidance embedded as a soft Artificial Potential Fields (APF) cost term respecting unicycle kinematics. A unified impedance-admittance controller executes these trajectories compliantly at 50 Hz for both the arms and the mobile base.

The main contributions of this work are:

  • •

    A Unified Cyber-Physical Framework: The first integration of a VLM-RAG module with whole-body MPC and unified virtual impedance-admittance control for bimanual mobile manipulation.

  • •

    Semantic-to-Physical Parameter Grounding: A pipeline where the VLM generates interpretable physical constraints (velocity, safety margins, and compliance gains) from scene semantics alone.

  • •

    Holistic Compliance Formulation: A unified framework applying a consistent spring-damper formulation to both manipulation and navigation, with obstacle avoidance embedded via an APF cost in the MPC.

  • •

    Experience-Driven Adaptation: A self-improving memory mechanism via ChromaDB that enables the robot to retrieve proven parameter sets for similar tasks without VLM fine-tuning.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III presents the system overview. Section IV details the methodology. Section V reports experimental results. Section VI concludes the paper.

II Related Work

II-A Vision-Language Models for Robot Planning

VLMs have emerged as powerful semantic front-ends for robotic systems. HYPERmotion [1] uses a VLM to select robot morphology and action primitives, coupling this to a motion library and MPC for physically consistent execution. VoxAct-B [14] leverages VLMs to assign roles to each arm in bimanual tasks based on language goals. RoboMIND 2.0 [2] provides a multimodal bimanual dataset of over 310,000 dual-arm trajectories, training a hierarchical VLM planner for grounded subgoal decomposition. MoManipVLA [5] and FALCON [6] further couple foundation models with whole-body MPC for loco-manipulation. Despite this progress, none of these systems use the VLM to generate compliance parameters — stiffness, damping, or velocity constraints — that directly shape physical interaction behavior.

II-B Whole-Body MPC for Mobile Manipulation

Whole-body MPC has enabled agile movements on high-DoF platforms, ranging from quadrupedal loco-manipulation  [7, 9] to task-priority transitions in mobile robots  [8]. However, in these frameworks, the safety margins (dsafed_{\text{safe}}) and velocity envelopes are static. Our work introduces a dynamic constraint-scaling mechanism where the human proximity detected by the VLM and directly dictates the MPC constraints.

II-C Impedance and Compliant Interaction

Since Hogan’s foundational work [15], virtual spring-damper formulations have underpinned compliant interaction. Recent efforts have optimized impedance for precision-compliance tradeoffs [3] and dual-arm coordination  [4]. DA-VIL [16] combined reinforcement learning with variable impedance for dual-arm coordination. While SafeHumanoid  [11] validated VLM-driven impedance scheduling for tabletop tasks, it was limited to single-arm systems. GenerativeMPC advances the state-of-the-art by unifying the impedance-admittance formulation across the entire mobile platform—base and arms—allowing for a singular, mathematically consistent approach to safe, context-aware co-habitation.

III SYSTEM OVERVIEW

III-A Hardware Platform

The platform consists of a 22 kg differential-drive base (wheel radius r=0.085r=0.085 m, and wheelbase L=0.455L=0.455 m) with two 6-DoF manipulators actuated by Feetech STS3215 servos [17] on two independent serial buses (Fig. 4). A Velodyne VLP-16 LiDAR and a RealSense D435 RGB-D camera provide obstacle point clouds and visual input to the VLM layer, respectively (Fig. 5). All computation runs onboard an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (16 GB) under ROS 2 Humble.

III-B Three-Layer Architecture

GenerativeMPC organizes control into three hierarchical layers illustrated in Fig. 3: VLM-RAG for semantic parameter generation, Whole-Body MPC for trajectory optimization at 10 Hz over N=7N=7 steps, and Impedance-Admittance for compliant tracking at 50 Hz. Completed episodes are stored in ChromaDB and retrieved to inform future VLM queries.

III-C Simulation and Sim-to-Real

Robot models were designed in SolidWorks and exported as URDF (Unified Robot Description Format), from which MuJoCo MJCF (MuJoCo XML model format) and IsaacSim USD (Universal Scene Description) files were derived, preserving link geometry, inertial properties, and joint limits. A MuJoCo warehouse scene was used for controller development and an IsaacSim environment for photorealistic sensor validation. The unified simulation loop executes MPC, impedance controller, and physics engine within a single 50 Hz callback, eliminating inter-process latency. For real-robot deployment, the architecture separates into ROS 2 nodes, revealing a sim-to-real gap from 30–60 ms Modbus RTU latency that required systematic gain reduction, documented in Table I.

IV METHODOLOGY

IV-A Layer 1: VLM-RAG Task Planning

The VLM-RAG layer translates natural language instructions and RGB-D imagery into actionable control parameters. An edge-deployed model (InternVL3-1B, INT4-quantized) processes the task instruction and produces a structured JSON description covering task type, detected objects, human presence, and proximity. This description is embedded and matched against ChromaDB via cosine similarity, retrieving validated parameter sets from prior executions under semantically similar conditions. The retrieval produces two distinct outputs: velocity limits vmaxv_{\max}, ωmax\omega_{\max} and safety margin dsafed_{\text{safe}} for the MPC, and stiffness KiK_{i} and damping DiD_{i} gains for the impedance-admittance controller. For instance, detecting a human within 1.5 m triggers a conservative profile (vmax=0.10v_{\max}=0.10 m/s, Ki=8.0K_{i}=8.0), whereas free-space navigation recovers nominal parameters. Completed episodes are written back to ChromaDB, enriching the database without VLM fine-tuning.

IV-B Layer 2: Whole-Body MPC

IV-B1 State and Control Representation

The state vector 𝐱∈ℝ9\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{9} collects base pose and both end-effector positions:

𝐱=[x,y,θ,𝐩L⊤,𝐩R⊤]⊤,\mathbf{x}=[x,\,y,\,\theta,\,\mathbf{p}_{L}^{\top},\,\mathbf{p}_{R}^{\top}]^{\top}, (1)

where (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta) is the base pose and 𝐩L,𝐩R∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{L},\mathbf{p}_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} are end-effector (EE) positions in the base frame. The control vector 𝐮∈ℝ8\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{8} is:

𝐮=[v,ω,𝐩˙L⊤,𝐩˙R⊤]⊤.\mathbf{u}=[v,\,\omega,\,\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{L}^{\top},\,\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{R}^{\top}]^{\top}. (2)

Task-space arm references allow the admittance layer and IK to absorb base drift and joint limit proximity without replanning.

IV-B2 Dynamics Model

The base is modeled as a unicycle:

[xk+1yk+1θk+1]=[xk+vkcosθkΔtyk+vksinθkΔtθk+ωk​Δ​t],\begin{bmatrix}x_{k+1}\\ y_{k+1}\\ \theta_{k+1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{k}+v_{k}\cos\theta_{k}\,\Delta t\\ y_{k}+v_{k}\sin\theta_{k}\,\Delta t\\ \theta_{k}+\omega_{k}\,\Delta t\end{bmatrix}, (3)

and each end-effector obeys 𝐩k+1=𝐩k+𝐩˙k​Δ​t\mathbf{p}_{k+1}=\mathbf{p}_{k}+\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{k}\,\Delta t, where kk denotes the time step index.

IV-B3 Cost Function

The MPC minimizes over N=7N=7 steps (Δ​t=0.15\Delta t=0.15 s):

J=Jterminal+Jrunning+Jobs+Jctrl+Jsmooth.J=J_{\text{terminal}}+J_{\text{running}}+J_{\text{obs}}+J_{\text{ctrl}}+J_{\text{smooth}}. (4)

where JobsJ_{\text{obs}} denotes the obstacle avoidance cost, detailed in (7). The terminal cost penalizes residual pose and end-effector errors at the horizon end:

Jterminal=wp​‖𝐩N−𝐩goal‖2+wθ​(θN−θgoal)2+warm​∑i∈{L,R}‖𝐩i,N−𝐩i,goal‖2,\begin{split}J_{\mathrm{terminal}}=\;&w_{p}\|\mathbf{p}_{N}-\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{goal}}\|^{2}+\;w_{\theta}(\theta_{N}-\theta_{\mathrm{goal}})^{2}\\ +\;&w_{\mathrm{arm}}\sum_{i\in\{L,R\}}\|\mathbf{p}_{i,N}-\mathbf{p}_{i,\mathrm{goal}}\|^{2},\end{split} (5)

where 𝐩N\mathbf{p}_{N} is the base position at the horizon end, 𝐩goal\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{goal}} is the target base position, and 𝐩i,N\mathbf{p}_{i,N} is the end-effector position of arm i∈{L,R}i\in\{L,R\} at the horizon end with 𝐩i,goal\mathbf{p}_{i,\mathrm{goal}} its target. The running cost promotes continuous progress through a progress-weighted path term and a heading alignment cost Jhdg,kJ_{\mathrm{hdg},k}, which transitions from angle-to-goal when the base is far (>>0.5 m) to the goal heading when close:

Jrunning=∑k=1Nwpath​kN​‖𝐩k−𝐩goal‖2+Jhdg,k.J_{\text{running}}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}w_{\text{path}}\frac{k}{N}\|\mathbf{p}_{k}-\mathbf{p}_{\text{goal}}\|^{2}+J_{\text{hdg},k}. (6)

Obstacle avoidance enters through a Khatib APF [18]:

Urep​(𝐱k)={η2​(1ρ⁡(𝐱k)−1ρ0)2ρ⁡(𝐱k)≤ρ00otherwise,U_{\mathrm{rep}}(\mathbf{x}_{k})=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\eta}{2}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\rho(\mathbf{x}_{k})}-\dfrac{1}{\rho_{0}}\right)^{2}&\rho(\mathbf{x}_{k})\leq\rho_{0}\\[8.0pt] 0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (7)

where ρ0=0.5\rho_{0}=0.5 m and η=50\eta=50. The potential fades to zero within 0.5 m of the goal to prevent local minima. This design choice reflects a fundamental constraint of differential-drive bases: lateral repulsive forces are projected out by the nonholonomic constraint, so avoidance must be planned rather than reacted to. Control effort and smoothness penalties are:

Jctrl=∑k=1N(wv​vk2+wω​ωk2+wp˙​∑i‖𝐩˙i,k‖2),J_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\!\left(w_{v}v_{k}^{2}+w_{\omega}\omega_{k}^{2}+w_{\dot{p}}\sum_{i}\|\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{i,k}\|^{2}\right), (8)
Jsmooth=∑k=1N[wΔ​v​(vk−vk−1)2+wΔ​ω​(ωk−ωk−1)2+wΔ​p˙∑i∥Δ𝐩˙i,k∥2],\begin{split}J_{\mathrm{smooth}}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\Big[&w_{\Delta v}(v_{k}-v_{k-1})^{2}+w_{\Delta\omega}(\omega_{k}-\omega_{k-1})^{2}\\ +\;&w_{\Delta\dot{p}}\sum_{i}\|\Delta\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{i,k}\|^{2}\Big],\end{split} (9)

where Δ​vk=vk−vk−1\Delta v_{k}=v_{k}-v_{k-1}, Δ​ωk=ωk−ωk−1\Delta\omega_{k}=\omega_{k}-\omega_{k-1}, and Δ​𝐩˙i,k=𝐩˙i,k−𝐩˙i,k−1\Delta\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{i,k}=\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{i,k}-\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{i,k-1} are the step-to-step changes in linear velocity, angular velocity, and end-effector velocity, respectively.

The problem is solved at 10 Hz via SLSQP (Sequential Least Squares Programming), warm-started from the previous solution. Key parameters are in Table II.

IV-C Layer 3: Unified Impedance-Admittance Control

IV-C1 Base and Arm Tracking

For both the mobile base and the arm end-effectors, a virtual impedance force is computed from the error between the MPC reference and the measured state:

𝐅virt=𝐃i​(𝐱˙d−𝐱˙)+𝐊i​(𝐱d−𝐱),\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{virt}}=\mathbf{D}_{i}(\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{d}-\dot{\mathbf{x}})+\mathbf{K}_{i}(\mathbf{x}_{d}-\mathbf{x}), (10)

where 𝐊i\mathbf{K}_{i} and 𝐃i\mathbf{D}_{i} are supplied at runtime by the VLM-RAG module. This force is passed through an admittance filter:

𝐱˙c=𝐱˙d+𝐃a−1​(𝐅virt−𝐊a​(𝐱c−𝐱d)),\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{c}=\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{d}+\mathbf{D}_{a}^{-1}\!\left(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{virt}}-\mathbf{K}_{a}(\mathbf{x}_{c}-\mathbf{x}_{d})\right), (11)

integrated as 𝐱c:=𝐱c+𝐱˙c​Δ​t\mathbf{x}_{c}:=\mathbf{x}_{c}+\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{c}\,\Delta t. For the base, the corrected velocity projects into the robot frame as vc=cos⁡θ​x˙c+sin⁡θ​y˙cv_{c}=\cos\theta\,\dot{x}_{c}+\sin\theta\,\dot{y}_{c}, with heading regulated by ωc=kθ​wrap​(θd−θ)\omega_{c}=k_{\theta}\,\mathrm{wrap}(\theta_{d}-\theta) and a near-goal blending scheme below 0.3 m. Wheel speeds follow:

ωR=vc+L2​ωcr,ωL=vc−L2​ωcr.\omega_{R}=\frac{v_{c}+\frac{L}{2}\omega_{c}}{r},\qquad\omega_{L}=\frac{v_{c}-\frac{L}{2}\omega_{c}}{r}. (12)

For the arms, (10)–(11) are applied independently in 3D task space for each end-effector.

IV-C2 Arm IK and Self-Collision Avoidance

The corrected end-effector velocity is mapped to joint velocities through damped least-squares IK [15]:

𝐪˙=𝐉⊤​(𝐉𝐉⊤+λ2​𝐈)−1​𝐱˙c,m,\dot{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{J}^{\top}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top}+\lambda^{2}\mathbf{I})^{-1}\dot{\mathbf{x}}_{c,m}, (13)

with commands integrated as 𝐪cmd​(k+1)=𝐪cmd​(k)+𝐪˙​(k)​Δ​t\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{cmd}}(k{+}1)=\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{cmd}}(k)+\dot{\mathbf{q}}(k)\Delta t. Prior to IK, should the distance between corrected end-effector positions fall below dsafe=0.08d_{\mathrm{safe}}=0.08 m, the two references are symmetrically separated along their connecting vector.

The whole-body MPC optimizes base and arm trajectories simultaneously over a single horizon, naturally emphasizing base convergence at long range and arm convergence in proximity to the goal, without explicit phase switching.

V EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

V-A Simulation Setup

Experiments are conducted in MuJoCo and IsaacSim environments. The MuJoCo warehouse scene features shelving units, cylindrical obstacles, and human-shaped mannequins, as shown in Fig. 6. IsaacSim provides photorealistic validation of the manipulation pipeline, as shown in Fig. 2. The VLM-RAG module is seeded with five demonstration episodes covering free navigation, human-proximate navigation, and bimanual reaching.

V-B Task 1: Human-Aware Navigation

The robot navigates to (3.0, 2.0, 0∘)(3.0,\,2.0,\,0^{\circ}) with two human mannequins along the path. Upon detecting human proximity, the VLM-RAG module retrieves a conservative profile, reducing base velocity from vmax=0.25v_{\max}=0.25 to 0.10 m/s — a 60 % speed reduction — and raising damping from Di=15.0D_{i}=15.0 to 25.0, without any manual gain scheduling. The MPC converges to the goal with a position error of 7.8 mm and heading error of 1.4∘1.4^{\circ} at t=71.7t=71.7 s, as shown in Figs. 1 and 7. A transient heading spike of 176∘ near the goal reflects the MPC aligning the base from its approach heading to the target orientation, resolved smoothly by the admittance controller.

V-C Task 2: Human Hand Avoidance

Following base convergence, the robot executes a bimanual reaching task. Upon detection of a human hand entering the workspace, the VLM-RAG module retrieves a compliant profile (Ki=8.0K_{i}=8.0, Di=25.0D_{i}=25.0, dsafe=0.15d_{\mathrm{safe}}=0.15 m), slowing arm motion and increasing compliance. A minimum end-effector distance of 0.15 m from the hand is maintained throughout. When the hand departs, nominal parameters are restored automatically. End-effector errors remain below 2 mm after convergence, with no singularity events observed across all tested configurations.

V-D Hardware Validation

The physical platform navigates from (0, 0)(0,\,0) to (2.0,−1.0)(2.0,\,-1.0) m in a shared workspace with a human present, as shown in Fig. 1 (right). The Velodyne VLP-16 LiDAR feeds real-time obstacle point clouds into the MPC APF cost, enabling online obstacle avoidance. The controller converges to 17.5 mm position accuracy — a degradation from the 7.8 mm simulation result attributable entirely to 30–60 ms Modbus RTU latency, which required the systematic gain reduction documented in Table I. Table III summarises the performance across simulation and hardware.

VI CONCLUSION

This paper introduced GenerativeMPC, a hierarchical cyber-physical framework that bridges semantic scene understanding with compliant physical control for bimanual mobile manipulation. A VLM-RAG module derives task-appropriate velocity constraints and safety margins for the whole-body MPC, and stiffness and damping gains for the impedance-admittance controller, directly from camera imagery and natural language — without manual gain scheduling or controller retraining. The MPC plans kinematically consistent trajectories with embedded APF obstacle avoidance, while the unified admittance framework applies a consistent spring-damper formulation to both arm compliance and base tracking. Experimental results confirm base navigation to 7.8 mm in simulation and 17.5 mm on hardware, a 60 % speed reduction near humans, and bimanual end-effector convergence below 2 mm. The sim-to-real gap is fully attributable to Modbus communication latency rather than controller design, as evidenced by the systematic gain reduction in Table I. Future work will focus on full bimanual manipulation validation on hardware, expansion of the ChromaDB episode database across more diverse task scenarios, and reduction of VLM inference latency toward faster semantic-to-physical parameter adaptation.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
